claim: Sporadic venous malformation (VM) and angiomatosis of soft tissue (AST) are benign, congenital vascular anomalies affecting venous vasculature.
source: Sporadic venous malformation (VM) and angiomatosis of soft tissue (AST) are benign, congenital vascular anomalies affecting venous vasculature.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about VM and AST that is supported by established medical knowledge and classification systems.

claim: Symptoms of VM and AST vary from motility disturbances to pain and disfigurement depending on the size and location of the lesion.
source: Depending on the size and location of the lesion, symptoms vary from motility disturbances to pain and disfigurement.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by established medical knowledge about these conditions.

claim: VM and AST lesions have high recurrence rates.
source: Due to the high recurrence of the lesions, more effective therapies are needed.
evidence: This statement is supported by clinical knowledge about the natural history of these lesions.

claim: TGFA is expressed and secreted in endothelial cells or intervascular stromal cells in AST and VM lesions.
source: We report, for the first time, the expression and secretion of transforming growth factor A (TGFA) in ECs or intervascular stromal cells in AST and VM lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry, RT-qPCR, and ELISA experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: TGFA induces secretion of VEGF-A in a paracrine fashion.
source: TGFA induced secretion of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF-A) in paracrine fashion, and regulated EC proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ELISA and cell culture experiments showing VEGF-A secretion after TGFA stimulation.

claim: TGFA regulates endothelial cell proliferation.
source: TGFA induced secretion of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF-A) in paracrine fashion, and regulated EC proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from IncuCyte proliferation assays and fibrin bead assays.

claim: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant p.H1047R increases TGFA expression.
source: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant in p.H1047R, a common somatic mutation found in these lesions, increased TGFA expression, enrichment of hallmark hypoxia, and in a mouse xenograft model, lesion size, and vascularization.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-sequencing data and RT-qPCR validation from cells expressing PIK3CA H1047R.

claim: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant p.H1047R increases enrichment of hallmark hypoxia.
source: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant in p.H1047R, a common somatic mutation found in these lesions, increased TGFA expression, enrichment of hallmark hypoxia, and in a mouse xenograft model, lesion size, and vascularization.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing data from PIK3CA H1047R-expressing cells.

claim: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant p.H1047R increases lesion size in a mouse xenograft model.
source: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant in p.H1047R, a common somatic mutation found in these lesions, increased TGFA expression, enrichment of hallmark hypoxia, and in a mouse xenograft model, lesion size, and vascularization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mouse xenograft experiments measuring lesion volume.

claim: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant p.H1047R increases vascularization in a mouse xenograft model.
source: Oncogenic PIK3CA variant in p.H1047R, a common somatic mutation found in these lesions, increased TGFA expression, enrichment of hallmark hypoxia, and in a mouse xenograft model, lesion size, and vascularization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemistry and histological scoring of CD31-stained sections.

claim: Afatinib treatment decreases vascularization in a mouse xenograft model with ECs expressing oncogenic PIK3CA p.H1047R variant and fibroblasts.
source: Treatment with afatinib, a pan-ErbB tyrosine-kinase inhibitor, decreased vascularization and lesion size in a mouse xenograft model with ECs expressing oncogenic PIK3CA p.H1047R variant and fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mouse xenograft experiments with afatinib treatment, including CD31 staining and histological scoring.

claim: Afatinib treatment decreases lesion size in a mouse xenograft model with ECs expressing oncogenic PIK3CA p.H1047R variant and fibroblasts.
source: Treatment with afatinib, a pan-ErbB tyrosine-kinase inhibitor, decreased vascularization and lesion size in a mouse xenograft model with ECs expressing oncogenic PIK3CA p.H1047R variant and fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mouse xenograft experiments measuring lesion volume after afatinib treatment.

claim: Targeting both intervascular stromal cells and endothelial cells is a potential treatment strategy for vascular lesions with a fibrous component.
source: Based on the data, we suggest that targeting of both intervascular stromal cells and ECs is a potential treatment strategy for vascular lesions having a fibrous component.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing the role of both cell types in lesion formation and response to afatinib treatment.

claim: VM lesions form due to a local defect in vascular development during embryogenesis.
source: Lesions form due to a local defect in vascular development during embryogenesis and expand with time, manifesting clinically usually in late childhood or early adulthood (Hassanein et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VM lesions expand with time and manifest clinically usually in late childhood or early adulthood.
source: Lesions form due to a local defect in vascular development during embryogenesis and expand with time, manifesting clinically usually in late childhood or early adulthood (Hassanein et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VM can locate in any tissue or internal organ and be either superficial or permeate multiple tissue planes.
source: VM can locate in any tissue or internal organ and be either superficial or permeate multiple tissue planes (Dompmartin et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: AST is typically found in extremities or trunks being subcutaneous or intramuscular.
source: whereas AST is typically found in extremities or trunks being subcutaneous or intramuscular.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by established medical knowledge.

claim: Overlapping magnetic resonance imaging findings but distinctive histological features are usually found between VM and AST.
source: Overlapping magnetic resonance imaging findings, but distinctive histological features, are usually found between VM and AST (Aronniemi et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In both AST and VM, venous structures form enlarged, irregular vascular channels.
source: In both AST and VM, venous structures form enlarged, irregular vascular channels (Aronniemi et al., 2017; Brouillard and Vikkula, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fibrous connective tissue with fibroblasts is detected around the various-sized vessels in AST.
source: Fibrous connective tissue with fibroblasts is detected around the various-sized vessels in AST (Aronniemi et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sclerotherapy can cause secondary fibrosis in VMs.
source: while sclerotherapy can cause secondary fibrosis in VMs (Aronniemi et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: VMs consist solely of venous structures.
source: Whereas VMs consists solely of venous structures, AST also has artery-like vessels, lymphatic vessels, small capillaries and mesenchymal tissue components, especially muscle-infiltrating fat (Aronniemi et al., 2017; Rao and Weiss, 1992)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: AST has artery-like vessels, lymphatic vessels, small capillaries and mesenchymal tissue components, especially muscle-infiltrating fat.
source: Whereas VMs consists solely of venous structures, AST also has artery-like vessels, lymphatic vessels, small capillaries and mesenchymal tissue components, especially muscle-infiltrating fat (Aronniemi et al., 2017; Rao and Weiss, 1992)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In sporadic VMs, somatic mutations in tyrosine-protein kinase receptor TEK are found in approximately half of the patients.
source: In sporadic VMs, somatic mutations in tyrosine-protein kinase receptor TEK are found in approximately half of the patients, while somatic PIK3CA mutations are found in 20% of the VMs lacking TEK alterations (Limaye et al., 2015; Soblet et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Somatic PIK3CA mutations are found in 20% of the VMs lacking TEK alterations.
source: In sporadic VMs, somatic mutations in tyrosine-protein kinase receptor TEK are found in approximately half of the patients, while somatic PIK3CA mutations are found in 20% of the VMs lacking TEK alterations (Limaye et al., 2015; Soblet et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Somatic PIK3CA mutations have been associated with AST.
source: Somatic PIK3CA mutations have also been associated with AST (Boccara et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Causative mutations in TEK and PIK3CA genes lead to chronic activation of AKT.
source: Causative mutations in these genes lead to chronic activation of AKT and dysregulation of EC migration, expression of angiogenic factors as well as alterations in composition and processing of the extracellular matrix (Limaye et al., 2015; Nätynki et al., 2015; Uebelhoer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Causative mutations in TEK and PIK3CA genes lead to dysregulation of EC migration.
source: Causative mutations in these genes lead to chronic activation of AKT and dysregulation of EC migration, expression of angiogenic factors as well as alterations in composition and processing of the extracellular matrix (Limaye et al., 2015; Nätynki et al., 2015; Uebelhoer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Causative mutations in TEK and PIK3CA genes lead to dysregulation of expression of angiogenic factors.
source: Causative mutations in these genes lead to chronic activation of AKT and dysregulation of EC migration, expression of angiogenic factors as well as alterations in composition and processing of the extracellular matrix (Limaye et al., 2015; Nätynki et al., 2015; Uebelhoer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Causative mutations in TEK and PIK3CA genes lead to alterations in composition and processing of the extracellular matrix.
source: Causative mutations in these genes lead to chronic activation of AKT and dysregulation of EC migration, expression of angiogenic factors as well as alterations in composition and processing of the extracellular matrix (Limaye et al., 2015; Nätynki et al., 2015; Uebelhoer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VM or AST do not regress spontaneously.
source: VM or AST do not regress spontaneously.
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by established medical knowledge.

claim: Symptomatic VM and AST lesions are treated with percutaneous sclerotherapy, percutaneous cryotherapy, endovascular laser treatment, or surgical resection when conservative treatment is ineffective.
source: If conservative treatment is ineffective, symptomatic lesions are treated with percutaneous sclerotherapy, percutaneous cryotherapy, endovascular laser treatment, or surgical resection (Rosenblatt, 2007; Steiner et al., 2013; Hage et al., 2018; Cornelis et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature describing treatment approaches.

claim: Sirolimus targeting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway is being tested in clinical trials for the treatment of VM.
source: At present, sirolimus targeting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway is tested in clinical trials for the treatment of VM (Adams et al., 2016; Boscolo et al., 2015) (ClinicalTrials.gov, study nro: NCT02638389).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and a clinical trial registration.

claim: Most previous studies on VM or AST pathogenesis have focused on the role of endothelial cells.
source: So far, most of the previous studies have been focused on the role of ECs in VM or AST pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the literature supported by general knowledge of the field.

claim: Targeting of stromal cells is an emerging concept for the development of anti-angiogenic therapies.
source: As targeting of stromal cells (SCs) is an emerging concept for the development of anti-angiogenic therapies (Bussard et al., 2016; Donnem et al., 2008; Criscitiello et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The median age of AST patients in the study cohort was 18 years (range 11-46 years).
source: Median age of the AST and VM patients was 18 (range 11–46 years, female-to-male ratio 14:6)
evidence: This is demographic data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: The female-to-male ratio in AST patients was 14:6.
source: Median age of the AST and VM patients was 18 (range 11–46 years, female-to-male ratio 14:6)
evidence: This is demographic data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: The median age of VM patients in the study cohort was 31 years (range 9-77 years).
source: and 31 (range 9–77 years female-to-male ratio 6:9), respectively.
evidence: This is demographic data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: The female-to-male ratio in VM patients was 6:9.
source: and 31 (range 9–77 years female-to-male ratio 6:9), respectively.
evidence: This is demographic data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: 85% of AST lesions are located in the extremities.
source: Most of the AST lesions (85%) are located in the extremities.
evidence: This is demographic data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: 60% of AST lesions were intramuscular lesions.
source: Of all AST lesions, 60% were intramuscular lesions (12/20)
evidence: This is demographic data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: 60% of VM lesions were from the extremities.
source: 60% of the VM lesions were from the extremities.
evidence: This is demographic data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: Oncogenic PIK3CA variants were detected in 19/38 patients (AST 75%, VM 18%).
source: Oncogenic PIK3CA variants were detected in 19/38 patients (AST 75%, VM 18%; Tables 1–2)
evidence: This is genetic data from the patient cohort obtained by droplet digital PCR.

claim: PIK3CA p.H1047R/L somatic mutation was found in 10/19 patients with oncogenic PIK3CA variants.
source: of which PIK3CA p.H1047R/L somatic mutation was found in 10/19 patients.
evidence: This is genetic data from the patient cohort obtained by droplet digital PCR.

claim: 53% of patients had received sclerotherapy.
source: 53% of patients had received sclerotherapy (VM 3/15, AST 15/20, VM/AST 2/3 patients, respectively).
evidence: This is clinical data from the patient cohort presented in the study.

claim: CD31-labeled longitudinal vessels in AST lesions are tortuous, branched, and variable in size.
source: CD31-labeled longitudinal vessels were shown to be torturous, branched, and variable in size (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy imaging of patient tissue samples.

claim: 1128 genes were differentially expressed between control cells and patient-derived CD31+ECs.
source: 1128 and 571 genes were found to be differentially expressed between control cells and patient-derived CD31+ECs, respectively (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is data from bulk RNA-sequencing analysis.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in patient-derived ECs are involved in cell proliferation, migration, extracellular matrix organization, and hypoxia.
source: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were involved in angiogenic cellular processes, such as cell proliferation, migration, extracellular matrix organization, and hypoxia (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is data from gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing results.

claim: Fourteen genes involved in ErbB signaling pathway were found to be differentially expressed in patient-derived ECs.
source: Of particular interest were the fourteen genes found to be involved in ErbB signaling pathway known to regulate pathological angiogenesis.
evidence: This is data from gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing results.

claim: Multiple ligands of ErbB1-4 receptors were detected in patient-derived ECs, including TGFA, AREG, neuregulin-1, and epigen.
source: Multiple ligands of ErbB1-4 receptors were detected, e.g., transforming growth factor A (TGFA), amphiregulin (AREG), neuregulin-1, and epigen (EPGN).
evidence: This is data from RNA-sequencing analysis of patient-derived ECs.

claim: G protein-coupled receptor signaling and RAS/MAPK cascade were found to be regulated in patient-derived ECs.
source: Also, G protein-coupled receptor signaling and RAS/MAPK cascade were found to be regulated (Figure 1C; Table 3)
evidence: This is data from gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing results.

claim: TGFA and amphiregulin were significantly upregulated in patient-derived CD31+ECs compared to control ECs.
source: Significant upregulation of ErbB1/EGFR ligands TGFA and amphiregulin (AREG) was validated by RT-qPCR in patient-derivedCD31+ECs in comparison to control ECs
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR validation experiments.

claim: No difference was observed in the regulation of EPGN between patient-derived and control ECs.
source: whereas no difference was observed in the regulation of ErbB4 ligand EPGN (Figure 1E; De Luca et al., 2008; Ginsberg, 2007).
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR validation experiments.

claim: Neuregulin-1 was downregulated in patient-derived CD31+ECs.
source: In accordance with data from bulk RNA-sequencing, ErbB2-ErbB4 binding neuregulin-1 was downregulated in patient-derived CD31+ECs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR validation experiments.

claim: E2F and FOSL1 were found to be major regulators of transcription activity in patient-derived ECs.
source: Cell cycle regulators E2F and FOSL1 were found to be the major regulators of transcription activity together with EC-specific transcription factor ERG (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is data from de novo motif analysis of regulatory regions.

claim: ERG was found to be a major regulator of transcription activity in patient-derived ECs.
source: Cell cycle regulators E2F and FOSL1 were found to be the major regulators of transcription activity together with EC-specific transcription factor ERG (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is data from de novo motif analysis of regulatory regions.

claim: TGFA mRNA was upregulated in both AST and VM lesions compared to control tissue.
source: TGFA mRNA was shown to be upregulated in both AST and VM by RT-qPCR (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, n=8 VM, n=3 AST) in comparison to control tissue
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR analysis of patient tissue samples.

claim: No change in AREG mRNA was observed in patient lesions compared to control tissue.
source: whereas no change of AREG mRNA was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR analysis of patient tissue samples.

claim: TGFA was detected in the endothelium, pericytes, and intervascular stromal cells in both AST and VM lesions by immunohistochemistry.
source: By immunohistochemistry, TGFA was detected in the endothelium, pericytes, and intervascular stromal cells in both AST and VM lesions (Figure 2B–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2; positivity in 4/5 VM, 9/10 AST, 1/1 VM/AST lesions).
evidence: This is data from immunohistochemistry experiments on patient tissue samples.

claim: Phosphorylated EGFR was detected in AST lesions, with most of the signal located in intervascular stromal cells.
source: Activated EGFR pathway was further demonstrated in AST lesions by detecting phosphorylated EGFR (positivity in 9/9 AST lesions; Figure 2D), with most of the signal located in intervascular stromal cells.
evidence: This is data from immunohistochemistry experiments on patient tissue samples.

claim: TGFA mRNA was upregulated in patient-derived CD31+ECs compared to control ECs.
source: In support of findings in immunohistochemistry, TGFA mRNA upregulation or secretion was detected in patient-derived CD31+ECs and in intervascular stromalCD31-, vimentin+ cells (Patient SCs; Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR experiments on patient-derived cells.

claim: TGFA secretion was detected in patient-derived intervascular stromal cells.
source: In support of findings in immunohistochemistry, TGFA mRNA upregulation or secretion was detected in patient-derived CD31+ECs and in intervascular stromalCD31-, vimentin+ cells (Patient SCs; Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is data from ELISA experiments on patient-derived cells.

claim: Patient stromal cells were characterized to be negative for CD31 marker and positive for vimentin.
source: By morphology patient SCs resembled fibroblasts, and (Figure 2F) were characterized by western blot to be negative for CD31 marker and positive for fibroblast and/or smooth muscle cell marker vimentin (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from western blot characterization of patient-derived cells.

claim: None of the patient stromal cells had PIK3CA mutations detected by ddPCR.
source: None of the patient SCs had PIK3CA mutations detected by ddPCR (Table 1).
evidence: This is data from droplet digital PCR analysis of patient-derived cells.

claim: Higher expression of EGFR mRNA was detected in control fibroblasts and patient stromal cells compared to endothelial cells.
source: Higher expression of EGFR mRNA was detected in control fibroblasts and patient SCs in comparison to ECs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR experiments on different cell types.

claim: TGFA mRNA expression was induced in PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs.
source: In-line with our experiments with patient-derived CD31+ECs, TGFA mRNA expression was shown to be induced in PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is data from RNA-sequencing and RT-qPCR validation of lentiviral-transduced cells.

claim: Hallmark mTORC1 signaling was detected in PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs.
source: In addition, GO analysis of these cells showed a hallmark 'mTORC1 signaling,' indicative of activation of the signaling pathway downstream from PIK3CA
evidence: This is data from gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing results.

claim: Hallmark Glycolysis was detected in PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs.
source: as well as hallmarks 'Glycolysis,' further indicative of a metabolic change from normal oxygen consumption towards anaerobic energy metabolism (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is data from gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing results.

claim: Hallmark hypoxia was detected as one of the top enriched hallmarks in PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs despite normoxic cell culture conditions.
source: Interestingly, despite the normoxic cell culture conditions, hallmark hypoxia was detected as one of the top enriched hallmarks in PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs by GO analysis (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is data from gene ontology analysis of RNA-sequencing results.

claim: Among 47 independent DEGs detected from patient-derived CD31+ECs under 'Response to hypoxia' or 'Hallmark Hypoxia,' the majority (28 DEGs) were significantly altered by HIF1A, HIF2A or oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R.
source: Further comparison to the RNA-sequencing data from ECs expressing constitutively active hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs; GSE98060) confirmed that among 47 independent DEGs detected from our patient-derived CD31+ECs (Figure 1) under 'Response to hypoxia' (GO: 0001666) or 'Hallmark Hypoxia,' the majority (28 DEGs) were significantly altered by HIF1A, HIF2A or oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R.
evidence: This is data from comparative analysis of RNA-sequencing datasets.

claim: Part of the HIF-regulated genes are direct transcriptional targets downstream of the oncogenic PIK3CA signaling.
source: This indicated that part of the HIF-regulated genes were also direct transcriptional targets downstream of the oncogenic PIK3CA signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap of gene expression patterns between HIF-expressing and PIK3CA H1047R-expressing cells.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between TGFA and HIF1A mRNA expression levels in patient lesions (ρ=0.73).
source: The data showed a strong positive correlation between TGFA and HIF1A mRNA expression levels (ρ=0.73)
evidence: This is data from correlation analysis of RT-qPCR results from patient tissue samples.

claim: There is a moderate correlation between TGFA and HIF2A mRNA expression levels in patient lesions (ρ=0.45).
source: and a moderate correlation between TGFA and HIF2A (ρ=0.45) (Figure 3C–D, n=12 AST, n=7 VM, n=2 VM/AST).
evidence: This is data from correlation analysis of RT-qPCR results from patient tissue samples.

claim: There is a positive correlation (ρ=0.62) between VEGFA and TGFA mRNA expression levels in patient lesions.
source: Additionally, a positive correlation (ρ=0.62) between VEGFA and TGFA mRNA expression levels (Figure 3E) was observed.
evidence: This is data from correlation analysis of RT-qPCR results from patient tissue samples.

claim: Patient stromal cells induce HUVEC sprouting without any additional growth factor stimulation.
source: Patient SCs were shown to induce HUVEC sprouting without any additional growth factor stimulation (Figure 4A–B), implying that paracrine factors secreted by the SCs modulate the EC phenotype.
evidence: This is data from fibrin bead angiogenesis assays.

claim: Paracrine factors secreted by patient stromal cells modulate the endothelial cell phenotype.
source: Patient SCs were shown to induce HUVEC sprouting without any additional growth factor stimulation (Figure 4A–B), implying that paracrine factors secreted by the SCs modulate the EC phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that patient SCs induce EC sprouting without exogenous growth factors.

claim: rhTGFA stimulation increases VEGFA mRNA expression in control fibroblasts.
source: Accordingly, a significant increase in VEGFA mRNA and protein secretion was observed after stimulation of control fibroblasts (HPF-c) with rhTGFA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data from RT-qPCR experiments on stimulated fibroblasts.

claim: rhTGFA stimulation increases VEGF-A protein secretion in control fibroblasts.
source: Accordingly, a significant increase in VEGFA mRNA and protein secretion was observed after stimulation of control fibroblasts (HPF-c) with rhTGFA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data from ELISA experiments on stimulated fibroblasts.

claim: Co-stimulation with rhVEGF-A and rhTGFA results in higher increase of EC area and sprouting compared to either growth factor alone.
source: Also, in a fibrin bead assay with HUVECs, co-stimulation with rhVEGF-A and rhTGFA proteins resulted in a higher increase of EC area and sprouting in comparison to either of the growth factors alone (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is data from fibrin bead angiogenesis assays with recombinant proteins.

claim: VEGF-A and TGFA have a synergistic effect on modulating EC phenotype.
source: This suggested that these growth factors have a synergistic effect on modulating EC phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that combined treatment with VEGF-A and TGFA produces greater effects than either alone.

claim: Co-culturing of PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs with HPF-c showed an increased growth rate compared to PIK3CAwt-treated cells.
source: Co-culturing of PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs together with HPF-c showed an increased growth rate in comparison to PIK3CAwt-treated cells.
evidence: This is data from IncuCyte live-cell imaging proliferation assays.

claim: The increased growth rate in PIK3CAH1047R expressing ECs co-cultured with HPF-c was abolished when TGFA expression in ECs was knocked down by siRNA.
source: Importantly, the response was abolished when TGFA expression in ECs was knocked down by siRNA (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from siRNA knockdown experiments combined with proliferation assays.

claim: TGFA expression is involved in PIK3CAH1047R-induced responses in EC-fibroblast co-cultures.
source: Importantly, the response was abolished when TGFA expression in ECs was knocked down by siRNA (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Thus, altogether the data suggests that TGFA expression, induced by oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R, results in a pro-angiogenic EC phenotype by increasing cell proliferation and VEGF-A secretion but only in conditions where ECs and HPF-c/SCs are combined.
evidence: This is an inference based on the siRNA knockdown experiments showing that TGFA is necessary for the observed effects.

claim: TGFA expression induced by oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R results in a pro-angiogenic EC phenotype by increasing cell proliferation and VEGF-A secretion only when ECs and HPF-c/SCs are combined.
source: Thus, altogether the data suggests that TGFA expression, induced by oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R, results in a pro-angiogenic EC phenotype by increasing cell proliferation and VEGF-A secretion but only in conditions where ECs and HPF-c/SCs are combined.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental observations including proliferation assays, ELISA, and siRNA knockdown experiments.

claim: Lesion growth and size at day 20 was similar between PIK3CAH1047R-transduced ECs with or without fibroblasts.
source: Lesion growth and size at d20 was observed to be similar between PIK3CAH1047R-transduced ECs with or without fibroblasts (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is data from mouse xenograft experiments measuring lesion volume.

claim: Various sized vascular channels filled with erythrocytes were detected in explants from the mouse xenograft model.
source: With H&E staining, various sized vascular channels filled with erythrocytes were detected (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is data from histological analysis of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: There was very little if any blood-filled vascularization in explants with ECs expressing PIK3CAwt.
source: Notably, there was very little if any blood-filled vascularization shown in explants with ECs expressing PIK3CAwt
evidence: This is data from histological analysis of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: Vascular channels in explants with PIK3CAwt expressing ECs and fibroblasts clearly contained erythrocytes.
source: whereas vascular channels in explants with PIK3CAwt expressing ECs and fibroblasts clearly contained erythrocytes (Figure 5C–D H).
evidence: This is data from histological analysis of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: Higher vascularization was observed in explants with embedded fibroblasts compared to ECs alone.
source: Higher vascularization, detected with EC marker CD31, was observed with explants with embedded fibroblasts in comparison to ECs alone (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is data from immunohistochemistry and scoring of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: Vascular channels with fibroblasts were wider and appeared more irregular in shape compared to explants containing only PIK3CAH1047R ECs.
source: In comparison to explants containing only PIK3CAH1047R ECs, the vascular channels with fibroblasts were wider and appeared more irregular in shape (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is data from histological and immunohistochemical analysis of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: The highest CD31 vascularization score and erythrocyte amount were detected in explants with ECs expressing PIK3CAH1047R and fibroblasts.
source: The highest CD31 vascularization score and erythrocyte amount were detected in explants with ECs expressing PIK3CAH1047R and fibroblasts (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: This is data from histological scoring and quantification of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: A higher number of inflammatory cells was seen in explants with ECs expressing PIK3CAH1047R than PIK3CAwt.
source: In addition, a higher number of inflammatory cells was seen in the explants with ECs expressing PIK3CAH1047R than PIK3CAwt; however, no statistical difference was detected with or without fibroblasts (Figure 5).
evidence: This is data from histological scoring of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: Fibroblasts are important for inducing aberrant vasculature in lesions.
source: In summary, the data indicates the importance/potential of fibroblasts in inducing aberrant vasculature in lesions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mouse xenograft experiments showing increased vascularization when fibroblasts are present.

claim: Afatinib blocks TGFA-stimulated EGFR phosphorylation.
source: First, in vitro, afatinib was shown to block TGFA-stimulated EGFR phosphorylation detected by western blot (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is data from western blot experiments with afatinib treatment.

claim: Afatinib decreases VEGF-A secretion from TGFA-stimulated control fibroblasts.
source: and to decrease VEGF-A secretion from TGFA-stimulated control fibroblasts measured by ELISA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is data from ELISA experiments with afatinib treatment.

claim: Afatinib reduces rhVEGF-A and rhTGF-A mediated EC sprouting in the fibrin bead assay.
source: Accordingly, in the fibrin bead assay, afatinib was shown to reduce rhVEGF-A and rhTGF-A mediated EC sprouting (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is data from fibrin bead angiogenesis assays with afatinib treatment.

claim: Afatinib treatment reduces lesion size in a mouse xenograft model with ECs expressing oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R and genotypically normal primary fibroblasts.
source: At d18, lesion size (Figure 7B–C) and vascularization detected by H&E and CD31 stainings (Figure 7H–L) was shown to be reduced in afatinib-treated mice in comparison to untreated mice.
evidence: This is data from mouse xenograft experiments with afatinib treatment.

claim: Afatinib treatment reduces vascularization in a mouse xenograft model with ECs expressing oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R and genotypically normal primary fibroblasts.
source: At d18, lesion size (Figure 7B–C) and vascularization detected by H&E and CD31 stainings (Figure 7H–L) was shown to be reduced in afatinib-treated mice in comparison to untreated mice.
evidence: This is data from mouse xenograft experiments with afatinib treatment and histological analysis.

claim: A lower number of inflammatory cells was detected in the afatinib treatment group compared to untreated mice.
source: A lower number of inflammatory cells was detected in the afatinib treatment group (Figure 7K).
evidence: This is data from histological scoring of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: A reduction of EGFR expression was detected in explants of afatinib-treated mice.
source: Accordingly, a reduction of EGFR expression was detected in explants of afatinib-treated mice (Figure 7 M).
evidence: This is data from immunohistochemistry and scoring of mouse xenograft explants.

claim: ErbB signaling plays a key role in PIK3CAH1047R lesion formation in the presence of fibroblasts.
source: Altogether, the data validates that ErbB signaling plays a key role in PIK3CAH1047R lesion formation in the presence of fibroblasts and provides a new potential therapeutic strategy for targeting vascular lesions with a fibrous component.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the afatinib treatment experiments showing reduced lesion formation when ErbB signaling is inhibited.

claim: Afatinib provides a new potential therapeutic strategy for targeting vascular lesions with a fibrous component.
source: Altogether, the data validates that ErbB signaling plays a key role in PIK3CAH1047R lesion formation in the presence of fibroblasts and provides a new potential therapeutic strategy for targeting vascular lesions with a fibrous component.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing efficacy of afatinib in reducing lesion size and vascularization.

claim: PIK3CA mutations were detected for the first time in ECs isolated from AST lesions.
source: Somatic mutations in PIK3CA were detected by ddPCR in lesions from 3 out of 5 patients (fractional abundance 44–51%, Tables 1–2), and for the first time, in ECs isolated from AST lesions (Table 1).
evidence: This is data from droplet digital PCR analysis of patient-derived cells.

claim: Oncogenic PIK3CA variants were detected in 75% of AST lesions.
source: Our study is the first to demonstrate PIK3CA mutations also in ECs isolated from AST. Oncogenic PIK3CA variants were detected in our study in the majority of AST lesions (75%, 15/20 patients)
evidence: This is data from droplet digital PCR analysis of patient tissue samples.

claim: A novel somatic mutation in PIK3CA, p.H1047L, was detected in AST.
source: Additionally, we detected in this study a novel somatic mutation in PIK3CA, p.H1047L, in AST.
evidence: This is data from droplet digital PCR analysis of patient tissue samples.

claim: TGFA is a known pro-angiogenic growth factor.
source: We demonstrate here for the first time that TGFA, a known pro-angiogenic growth factor (De Luca et al., 2008; Leker et al., 2009; Schreiber et al., 1986), is upregulated in VM and AST lesions
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TGFA is upregulated in VM and AST lesions in the presence of an oncogenic PIK3CA variant.
source: We demonstrate here for the first time that TGFA, a known pro-angiogenic growth factor (De Luca et al., 2008; Leker et al., 2009; Schreiber et al., 1986), is upregulated in VM and AST lesions, and in the presence of an oncogenic PIK3CA variant.
evidence: This is data from RNA-sequencing, RT-qPCR, and immunohistochemistry experiments.

claim: TGFA and EGFR are located in both intervascular stromal cells and the endothelium in patient lesions.
source: TGFA and its receptor EGFR are located in both intervascular stromal cells and the endothelium.
evidence: This is data from immunohistochemistry experiments on patient tissue samples.

claim: Patient stromal cells are able to secrete TGFA and VEGF-A.
source: We further demonstrated that patient SCs were able to: (i) secrete TGFA and VEGF-A; and (ii) transform genotypically normal ECs toward a pro-angiogenic phenotype.
evidence: This is data from ELISA experiments on patient-derived cells.

claim: Patient stromal cells transform genotypically normal ECs toward a pro-angiogenic phenotype.
source: We further demonstrated that patient SCs were able to: (i) secrete TGFA and VEGF-A; and (ii) transform genotypically normal ECs toward a pro-angiogenic phenotype.
evidence: This is data from fibrin bead angiogenesis assays.

claim: Genotypically normal fibroblasts increase lesion vascularization and erythrocyte amount when used together with human ECs expressing PIK3CA isoforms in a mouse xenograft model.
source: Accordingly, our experiments in a modified mouse xenograft model showed an increase in lesion vascularization and erythrocyte amount when genotypically normal fibroblasts were used together with human ECs expressing PIK3CA isoforms.
evidence: This is data from mouse xenograft experiments with histological analysis.

claim: Afatinib is an irreversible inhibitor of EGFR/ErbB1, ErbB2, and ErbB4.
source: We also demonstrated that afatinib, an irreversible inhibitor of EGFR/ErbB1, ErbB2, and ErbB4, was able to decrease PIK3CAH1047R-induced lesion growth and vascularization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of action of afatinib.

claim: Afatinib decreases PIK3CAH1047R-induced lesion growth and vascularization.
source: We also demonstrated that afatinib, an irreversible inhibitor of EGFR/ErbB1, ErbB2, and ErbB4, was able to decrease PIK3CAH1047R-induced lesion growth and vascularization.
evidence: This is data from mouse xenograft experiments with afatinib treatment.

claim: ErbB signaling induces activation of RAS/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways that are involved in cell proliferation and inhibition of apoptosis.
source: As ErbB signaling has been shown to induce activation of RAS/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways that are involved in cell proliferation and inhibition of apoptosis (Zong et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Targeting both ECs and intervascular stromal cells by pharmacological agents could be beneficial to increase treatment response in patients with VM or AST having a fibrous component.
source: As ErbB signaling has been shown to induce activation of RAS/MAPK and PI3K/Akt pathways that are involved in cell proliferation and inhibition of apoptosis (Zong et al., 2017), targeting of both ECs and intervascular SCs by pharmacological agents could be beneficial to increase treatment response in patients with VM or AST having a fibrous component.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and cited literature about ErbB signaling pathways.

claim: Hypoxic avascular stromal cells regulate angiogenesis.
source: Previously, hypoxic avascular stromal cells were suggested to regulate angiogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings supported by general knowledge of the field.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts can induce tumor initiation, progression, and angiogenesis by producing growth factors, proteases, chemokines, and extracellular matrix.
source: For example, cancer-associated fibroblasts can induce tumor initiation, progression, and angiogenesis by producing growth factors, proteases, chemokines, and extracellular matrix (Kalluri, 2016; Watnick, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fibroblasts modulate EC/pericyte migration and are crucial for lumen formation.
source: Fibroblasts have also been shown to modulate EC/pericyte migration, and to be crucial for lumen formation.
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings supported by general knowledge of the field.

claim: Fibroblasts are the main source of VEGF-A production in cancer.
source: They are also the main source of VEGF-A production in cancer (Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Perturbation of VEGFR signaling is linked to most vascular anomalies.
source: Perturbation of VEGFR signaling is linked to most vascular anomalies and has been demonstrated for example in infantile hemangioma and arteriovenous malformation (Chang et al., 1999; Koizumi et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Current treatment strategies targeting cancer-associated fibroblasts aim to inhibit secretion of pro-angiogenic growth factors, reduce accumulation of cells to tumor microenvironment, and inhibit expression of lysyl oxidase-like proteins.
source: Current treatment strategies targeting cancer-associated fibroblasts aim to: (i) inhibit secretion of pro-angiogenic growth factors; (ii) reduce the accumulation of cells to tumor microenvironment via anti-fibrotic agents; and (iii) inhibit expression of lysyl oxidase-like proteins that regulate ECM integrity (Puré and Lo, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cancer cells are genetically unstable by accruing mutations that allow escape from cellular regulatory mechanisms and enable development of drug resistance.
source: Whereas cancer cells are considered genetically instable by accruing mutations that allow escape from cellular regulatory mechanisms and enable the development of drug resistance, cancer-associated stromal cells are not typically mutated in cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Cancer-associated stromal cells are not typically mutated in cancer.
source: Whereas cancer cells are considered genetically instable by accruing mutations that allow escape from cellular regulatory mechanisms and enable the development of drug resistance, cancer-associated stromal cells are not typically mutated in cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: In VM, mutations in PIK3CA or TEK genes occur solely in EC fraction.
source: In VM, mutations in PIK3CA or TEK genes have been shown to occur solely in EC fraction (Goines et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PIK3CA mutations were detected only in the EC fraction of AST lesions.
source: We also detected PIK3CA mutations only in the EC fraction of AST lesions.
evidence: This is data from droplet digital PCR analysis of patient-derived cells.

claim: Lesion-derived intervascular stromal cells secrete pro-angiogenic growth factors that can change genotypically normal EC function and enable angiogenesis.
source: Besides the clear role of these mutations in ECs driving the lesion formation, we here demonstrate that lesion-derived intervascular SCs are able to secrete pro-angiogenic growth factors that can change genotypically normal EC function and enable angiogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from ELISA and fibrin bead assays.

claim: A hypoxic environment induces overexpression of EGFR in cancer.
source: Besides genetic factors, a hypoxic environment has been shown to induce overexpression of EGFR in cancer (Franovic et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A hypoxic environment upregulates both TGFA and VEGF-A in cancer and ECs.
source: and to upregulate both TGFA and VEGF-A in cancer and ECs (Gunaratnam et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Depletion of both HIF1A and HIF2A leads to downregulation of TGFA expression.
source: In addition, depletion of both HIF1A and HIF2A has previously been shown to lead to the downregulation of TGFA expression (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Some patients in the study had received sclerotherapy, which may have caused a hypoxic environment of cells.
source: As some of the patients used in this study had received sclerotherapy, the treatment may have caused a hypoxic environment of cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known effects of sclerotherapy and the patient treatment history.
